Current ideation absent; intent absent; plan absent; access reviewed true. Disposition: Outpatient care with close follow-up. She has no current thoughts of suicide or self-harm and no self-injury now; past self-injury at a time of great distress is part of her history and was discussed with her gently. Eating disorders and depression both raise the risk of suicide and self-harm, so a written safety plan was made with her, with her own warning signs (a run of bad nights of bingeing, feeling hopeless, or wanting to hurt herself) and what to do about each, including whom to call. Lethal-means counseling: no firearm and no access to one; medicines are kept in small amounts. The 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) was given and saved in her phone, with the clinic number. Safety reviewed at every visit.

text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Medical risk assessment and monitoring for purging: orthostatic vital signs and weight at every visit, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate and creatinine weekly until potassium is normal twice and then at each visit, magnesium and phosphate at baseline and when potassium is low, an ECG at baseline and after any QT-relevant medicine change while potassium is low, and urgent or inpatient care for potassium below 3.0 mmol/L despite replacement, QTc above 500 ms, fainting, a pulse below 50, or blood in the vomit
  • Eating disorders psychiatry consultation on the diagnosis and its severity, the right level of care, psychological treatment, fluoxetine, and medical monitoring
  • Oral potassium chloride 20 mEq twice daily, with a recheck in one week; stopped once potassium is normal and vomiting is less frequent
  • Nutrition: an eating disorders dietitian; regular eating of three meals and two or three snacks a day, no dieting or skipped meals, and no foods banned; caffeine cut down
  • Dental protection while vomiting continues: no brushing for an hour after vomiting, a non-acid fluoride mouthwash, fewer acidic drinks, and a dental examination
  • Structured safety assessment, a written safety plan with her warning signs, lethal-means counseling, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, the PHQ-9 at each visit, and safety review at every visit
  • Eating-disorder-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT-E): 20 sessions over 20 weeks with an eating disorders therapist, twice weekly for the first four weeks, with weighing in session, self-monitoring records, regular eating, work on shape and weight concerns and on binges triggered by difficult feelings, and a written relapse-prevention plan at the end
  • Fluoxetine started at 20 mg each morning and raised to 40 mg after one week and 60 mg after two weeks, for both the bulimia and the depression; ECG two weeks after reaching 60 mg; mood, sleep, agitation and suicidal thoughts checked at each visit; continued for at least a year after remission

resource.title: Diana, Princess of Wales synthetic care plan
resource.description: Respectful, unhurried primary care for a 28-year-old woman who asks for help with bulimia nervosa she has hidden for years: a structured eating-disorder assessment (SCOFF and EDE-Q) and DSM-5-TR severity grading; a medical risk assessment for purging (orthostatic vital signs, potassium, magnesium, phosphate and bicarbonate, an ECG with the QTc, and the parotid, dental and skin findings of vomiting), with oral potassium replacement and clear thresholds for a higher level of care; eating-disorder-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT-E) as first-line treatment with fluoxetine 60 mg daily, the medicine with the best evidence; nutrition built on regular eating; dental protection; measurement-based care for co-occurring depression; and a structured safety assessment with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline reviewed at every visit, on the APA 2023 eating disorders guideline, NICE NG69, and the CMID depression monograph.
